correctness.rationale: Every clique projects to three identical permutations in a hypothetical three-uniform word. Cyclic rotation and global column relabeling normalize the first row. Exhausting 24 permutations and C(23,11) interleavings produces exactly 354 pair patterns. Both complete implementations exhaust all 125,316 projection pairs and every within-gap merge, finding no full word. One enumerates 158,483,130 full merged projections; a separately coded bitmask automaton counts 238,188 shuffles obeying the four required matching alternations, none obeying the twelve nonedge constraints. The lower bound extends by induced-subgraph restriction. Broere--Zantema Section 5 provides the explicit four-word upper construction for all n; its substitution is separately checked for n=2 through 10. The finite exhaustive lemma, not experimental extrapolation, proves the universal claim. The induced Rook_{3,3}, with published representation number three, separately excludes one- and two-uniform representations, so ruling out three copies is sufficient.

evidence: Broere--Zantema, arXiv:1808.01800v1, Section 5 Theorem 1 and proof: if G has a k-uniform representation, k>1, then G Cartesian K_r has a (k+r-1)-uniform representation. For G=K_n, k=2 and r=3 this yields four, only as an upper bound.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The stronger-parameter product theorem is fully applicable but proves only existence of a four-uniform word; it does not exclude three-uniform words. There is no implication from a four-uniform construction to a minimum of four. The new exhaustive lower obstruction supplies the missing direction.
